rounds.proof_sketch: The mutation changes thread_max initialization from -FLT_MAX (~-3.4e38) to -1e10f in max_reduction_dim1_kernel. With input shape [16, 256, 256], dim1=256 elements are reduced. With block_size=256, elements_per_thread=(256+255)/256=1, so each thread processes exactly 1 element. If that element is < -1e10 (e.g., -1e15), original code: thread_max=-FLT_MAX, val(-1e15)>thread_max is TRUE, result=-1e15. Mutated code: thread_max=-1e10, val(-1e15)>thread_max is FALSE, result=-1e10. Difference = 9e14, far exceeding tolerance.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation only produces different behavior when input values are more negative than -1e10. All tested policies (all_negative, extreme_magnitude, etc.) used typical distributions: randn-based negative values range ~[-4, -0.1], extreme_magnitude likely focused on positive large values (~1e38). No test explicitly targeted extremely negative values below -1e10. The 'all_negative' policy likely used torch.randn scaled negatively, producing values nowhere near -1e10. The critical value range (-FLT_MAX, -1e10) was never exercised, allowing the mutant to survive.
rounds.kill_strategy: Create input tensor where ALL values along the reduction dimension (dim1) are less than -1e10 but representable as float32 (i.e., > -FLT_MAX). Values like -1e15, -1e20, or -1e30 will work. When the model reduces over dim=1, the original kernel correctly returns the maximum negative value, while the mutant incorrectly returns -1e10.
rounds.recommendations: When testing reduction kernels with identity-element mutations, explicitly test extreme negative values beyond typical distribution ranges. The 'all_negative' policy should include cases with values like -1e20 or -1e30, not just negated standard randn values. For max-reduction specifically, test the initialization boundary (-1e10 in this case) with values on both sides.

    # Create tensor with all values = -1e15, which is < -1e10 (mutant threshold)

    x = torch.full((16, 256, 256), -1e15, dtype=torch.float32, device=device)
